title: Open RTU: an open reference instrument for grid-side frequency compliance monitoring
abstract: Release v1.2.0 of Open RTU is the version cited by the manuscript "Replay Validation Against NESO Records: An Open Reference Instrument for Offshore Wind Frequency Compliance" (J. Davies, L. Kang, A. Hettiarachchige Don), in preparation to be submitted to MDPI Sensors. It contains: the measurement and generator firmware of the reported builds; the bill of materials (bom.csv); the SCADA HMI; the LTspice netlist of the conditioning model (hardware/); the NESO trajectories for the replayed events; every bench capture reported in the paper; the complete analysis toolchain. One command, python analysis/reproduce_all.py, runs from a clean clone started in any directory. It does the following in 14 steps: verifies the canonical capture's SHA-256; clears previous outputs so that no stale result can pass; recomputes the TOST equivalence, Bland–Altman, TVE-equivalent, sensitivity-sweep, replay, runtime, estimator-comparison, swing-equation and Cramér–Rao results, each checked against the value printed in the paper; verifies the derived-output hash quoted in the Data Availability Statement; checks every value in Tables 2–8 with paper_tables.py; redraws Figures 11–15, 17 and 18 with paper_figures.py. New in this release: The table and figure regeneration scripts (paper_tables.py, paper_figures.py). The real-sinusoid Cramér–Rao bound, evaluated at the measured 1816.5 Hz sampling rate. Its closed form is confirmed by Fisher-matrix inversion and by a fixed-seed Monte Carlo fit (crb_confirm.py). The Kalman noise-ratio sensitivity sweep (kalman_sweep.py). The Section 3.12 acquisition-chain characterisation: two bench sessions with their firmware, raw records, analysis scripts and the scripts that draw Figures 19 and 20. CITATION.cff, and requirements.txt giving the library versions that reproduce every derived output byte for byte. The manifest covers 203 files. Run python analysis/make_hashes.py --check to verify it. The raw V7.2 DMA capture (Figure 16, a negative result) is available from the corresponding author on request. Licence: GPL-3.0.

title: Compact models and the i-MOS platform developments for the tunneling field-effect transistor technology
abstract: Tunneling field-effect transistors (TFETs) based on the quantum interband tunneling are under extensive research. They provide one promising solution for the CMOS power problem due to the fast switching property with sub-60mV/dec subthreshold swing. Experimental studies on the TFETs structures and materials have been reported in literatures. However, the infrastructure for the research and developments of the TFETs technology is incomplete due to the lack of the electronic design automation (EDA) tools which support the TFETs based integrated circuit simulations and designs. This thesis is focused on developing the compact models and the i-MOS platform to fulfill the gap between the TFETs device and circuit designs. A compact model for TFETs with double-gate and nanowire configurations is developed in this thesis. With understandings of TFETs operations, unique properties of TFETs and their geometry dependences are identified. The source depletions and channel inversions responsible for the sub-60mV/dec subthreshold swing and the exponential segment in the output curves of TFETs are considered. A closed form solution of the tunneling current is proposed, capturing the main device physiys as well as reducing the computation complexity based on SPICE simulation considerations. A 100/0 channel charge partition scheme is proved based on which the terminal charge model is formulated to describe the capacitance characteristics. The geometry dependences of the double-gate and nanowire TFETs characteristics are reproduced by the compact model. The diffusive transport in TFETs is modeled by the proposed drain-FET method and source-resistance method. TFETs with the uniaxial strain engineering are also accounted for by combining the compact model and tight-binding simulations of material properties. To assist the TFETs based circuit designs, the i-MOS platform which serves the purpose of an EDA tool for the TFETs technology is developed. With an internet browser as the user interface, the i-MOS provides services from single device simulations, parameter extractions to circuit simulations. It is powered by the tailored open source Ngspice with the developed TFET model implemented. The web-based simulation system is constructed with the efficiently linked server side and client side programs. Simulations of TFETs based logic gates on i-MOS are demonstrated.

venue: ITEGAM- Journal of Engineering and Technology for Industrial Applications (ITEGAM-JETIA)
title: Performance-Driven Optimization of CMOS-Based Two-Stage Operational Amplifier Using Metaheuristic Algorithms
abstract: Design of CMOS based analog circuits becomes increasingly complex as transistor sizing plays a crucial role due to the trade-offs among power consumption, silicon area, unity gain bandwidth, slew rate, and open loop gain. This sizing challenge is makes analog circuit design inherently multi objective, and traditional analytical approaches based on simplified transistor level equations often fail to deliver globally optimal results. Metaheuristic optimization techniques have emerged as an effective alternative to explore nonlinear and multi-dimensional design spaces. In this work, the design of a two stage CMOS operational amplifier in the Predictive Technology Model (PTM) 45 nm technology node is optimized using four algorithms: Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), RAO algorithm, Teaching Learning Based Optimization (TLBO), and the proposed Modified TLBO (MTLBO). The algorithms were implemented in Python and verified through Ngspice-26 simulator on an AMD Ryzen™ processor with 16 GB RAM, 64 bit Ubuntu environment. The proposed MTLBO achieved 86.15 dB voltage gain, 94.05 dB CMRR, and 185 MHz unity gain bandwidth. Comparative analysis shows that the proposed MTLBO algorithm achieves faster convergence with fewer iterations and consistently outperforms PSO, RAO, and TLBO making it a strong candidate for efficient analog VLSI design automation.

title: Investigations of the Usefulness of Automated FMECAs for Electronic Circuits
abstract: The Failure Mode, Effects, and Criticality Analysis (FMECA) can be used to assess risks in safety-critical electronic circuits by systematically evaluating the impact of each component failure at the system level. FMECAs are traditionally carried out manually, focusing on individual component failure modes. Since certain failures may lead to severe system-level effects, it is essential to identify these failures, whether they occur before or during operation and whether individually or in combination. This makes it necessary to consider both the timing of failures and their interactions, factors which are difficult to address in manual FMECA but can be handled through automated approaches. Previous research on automating the analysis mainly focused on speeding up the process and avoiding incorrectly assigned system-level effects. While component failure timing can alter the effect, its automation has not yet been studied. Similarly, multi-component failures can lead to new system-level effects. However, previous work has mainly focused on reducing the number of combinations to make automation feasible, rather than analyzing their actual impact on reliability outcomes. This raises three key questions: How does failure timing influence system-level effects? What is the impact of multi-component failures on the outcome of a reliability analysis? What does this imply for the usefulness of an automated approach in a reliability assurance process? To answer these questions, three electronic systems were selected. Manual and automated FMECAs, the latter using LTspice and custom Python scripts, were performed and compared for each example. Results show that failure timing and multi-component failures can have a minor influence on system-level effects. Automation helps avoid incorrect effect assignments made by experts but still requires manual efforts to be set up. This implies that automation and analysis of the failure timing and interaction is primarily recommended for highly critical systems.

venue: DR-NTU (Nanyang Technological University)
title: Development of flutter apps for rectifier circuit analysis
abstract: This dissertation designs and implements a cross-platform circuit analysis application based on the Flutter framework. The application adopts a front-end and back-end separation architecture: the front-end uses Flutter to implement a visual circuit editing interface, while the back-end uses Python Flask to provide symbolic computation services. The main work is as follows: First, the overall architecture design, platform construction, and development environment configuration of the system are completed. Second, front-end core modules are implemented on the Flutter platform, including the circuit editing module, voltage source module, and result display module, supporting users in freely building circuit topologies, configuring component parameters, and viewing analysis results through a visual interface. Third, back-end core algorithms are implemented on the Python platform, including the construction and solution of the MNA matrix, state enumeration and self-consistency verification, and the State Space Averaging method, ultimately outputting a series of visualization results such as the transfer function. Finally, through comparative testing with the professional simulation software LTspice on identical circuit topologies, the functional completeness and computational accuracy of the application are verified. Keywords: Circuit analysis, Transfer function, Flutter, Modified Nodal Analysis

title: Adaptive Control and Simulation of a Transformer-Aided Full-Bridge Rectifier for Enhanced Piezoelectric Energy Harvesting in Smart Power Systems
abstract: Piezoelectric energy harvesting (PEH) offers a promising solution for powering low-power electronic devices in smart systems, but its effectiveness is often hampered by variable input vibrations and inherent impedance mismatch issues. This paper presents an innovative adaptive control and simulation framework designed to optimize energy extraction from piezoelectric sources. We propose a system integrating a piezoelectric transducer, a transformer for impedance matching, a full-bridge rectifier (FBR) for efficient AC-DC conversion, and an adaptive control strategy driven by a machine learning (ML) model. The transformer aids in stepping up the typically low piezoelectric voltage and matching the source impedance to the rectifier input impedance under varying conditions. The ML controller dynamically predicts optimal system parameters, specifically targeting the transformer’s effective turns ratio or configuration, based on real-time or simulated input characteristics. Detailed simulations using LTspice for circuit-level analysis and Python for ML model training and system-level simulation are presented. The framework demonstrates significant improvements in harvested power and output voltage stability compared to traditional fixed-parameter PEH systems. The novelty lies in the synergistic combination of transformer-based interfacing, FBR rectification, and ML-driven adaptive control, validated through a comprehensive simulation approach.

title: Averaged‐Switch Modeling and Simulation
abstract: Chapter 1 of Advanced Modeling and Control of DC-DC Converters presents a comprehensive introduction to averaged-switch modeling, focusing on the synchronous buck converter as a foundational example. It begins with a derivation of state-space equations, progresses through averaging techniques, and formulates dynamic models suitable for control design. The chapter explores practical applications, such as point-of-load voltage regulation, and evaluates control-to-output transfer functions using tools like MATLAB and Python. It also reviews fundamental control principles and feedback loop design concepts, laying the groundwork for robust closed-loop system analysis. Simulation plays a central role in this chapter, with hands-on examples using LTspice, PSIM, and MATLAB to validate models and design strategies. Key topics include loop gain analysis in both continuous and discontinuous conduction modes (CCM/DCM), output impedance modeling, and the incorporation of losses into averaged-switch frameworks. The chapter culminates with advanced modeling approaches, including null-double injection techniques and small-signal AC analysis in DCM. Through theory, simulation, and design verification, this chapter equips readers with the foundational tools and insights necessary to model and control DC-DC converters using averaged-switch techniques.
